summary.text: Assuming either prime family is bounded by \(N\), apply positivity at \(n=(N+2)!/6\) to obtain primes \(p=6x-1\) and \(q=6y+1\) with \((N+2)!=p+q\). In the Sophie Germain case \(p\le N\), while in the twin-prime case \(q-2\le N\); thus respectively \(p\) or \(q\) divides the factorial and hence the other prime, forcing equality (apart from the impossible divisor \(1\)), but \(6x-1=6y+1\) is impossible modulo \(6\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ and }2p+1\text{ are prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
T=\{p\in\mathbb N:p\text{ and }p+2\text{ are prime}\}
\]
be the set of smaller members of twin-prime pairs.

For a positive integer \(n\), the number \(a(n)=A227923(n)\) is the sum, over integers \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\), of an indicator which is \(1\) precisely when, on putting \(y=n-x\), all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
are prime. Notice that
\[
12x-1=2(6x-1)+1,
\]
so the first two primality conditions say exactly that \(6x-1\) is a Sophie Germain prime. The last two conditions say that \(6y-1\) and \(6y+1\) form a twin-prime pair.

Assume throughout that
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1.
\]
We prove that both \(S\) and \(T\) are infinite.

First observe the following immediate consequence of the definition of \(a(n)\). For every \(n>1\), there are integers \(x,y\ge 1\) such that
\[
x+y=n
\]
and
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\]
are all prime. Indeed, \(a(n)\) is a finite sum of terms each equal to either \(0\) or \(1\). If no \(x\) in the range \(1\le x<n\) satisfied all four conditions, every term would be zero and hence \(a(n)=0\), contrary to the hypothesis. For a qualifying \(x\), setting \(y=n-x\) gives \(y\ge1\).

We next package this observation into a factorial construction that will be used twice. Fix any integer \(N\ge3\), and put
\[
F=(N+2)!.
\]
Since \(N+2\ge5\), the factorial \(F\) is divisible by \(3!=6\). Thus there is an integer \(n\) such that
\[
F=6n.
\]
Moreover,
\[
F=(N+2)!\ge5!=120,
\]
so \(n\ge20\), in particular \(n>1\). Applying the assumed positivity of \(a(n)\) and the preceding witness-extraction observation, choose \(x,y\ge1\) with \(x+y=n\) for which
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\]
are all prime. Then
\[
(6x-1)+(6y+1)=6(x+y)=6n=F=(N+2)!.
\]
Consequently, for every \(N\ge3\), there exist \(x,y\ge1\) such that:

1. \(6x-1\) is a Sophie Germain prime, because both \(6x-1\) and
   \(2(6x-1)+1=12x-1\) are prime;
2. \(6y-1\) and \(6y+1\) are twin primes;
3. their cross-sum satisfies
   \[
   (6x-1)+(6y+1)=(N+2)!.
   \]

We now prove that the Sophie Germain primes are infinite. It is enough to show that \(S\) is not bounded above, since every finite set of natural numbers has an upper bound. Suppose, for contradiction, that \(S\) is bounded above by some integer \(N\); thus
\[
p\le N\qquad\text{for every }p\in S.
\]
The number \(5\) belongs to \(S\), since \(5\) and \(2\cdot5+1=11\) are both prime. Hence \(N\ge5\), and in particular \(N\ge3\), so the factorial construction applies.

Choose \(x,y\ge1\) as above, and abbreviate
\[
p=6x-1,\qquad q=6y+1.
\]
The construction gives
\[
p+q=(N+2)!,
\]
and both \(p\) and \(q\) are prime. Also \(p\in S\), because \(12x-1=2p+1\) is prime. By the assumed upper bound on \(S\),
\[
p\le N.
\]
Every positive integer at most \(N+2\) divides \((N+2)!\), so in particular
\[
p\mid (N+2)!.
\]
Of course \(p\mid p\). Subtracting \(p\) from the identity \((N+2)!=p+q\), we obtain
\[
p\mid q.
\]
Because \(q\) is prime, each positive divisor of \(q\) is either \(1\) or \(q\). Therefore either \(p=1\) or \(p=q\).

Neither possibility can occur. Since \(x\ge1\),
\[
p=6x-1\ge5,
\]
so \(p\ne1\). On the other hand, \(p=q\) would mean
\[
6x-1=6y+1,
\]
so
\[
6(x-y)=2,
\]
which is impossible for integers \(x,y\); equivalently, the left side is divisible by \(6\) and the right side is not. This contradiction proves that \(S\) has no upper bound and hence is infinite.

It remains to prove that there are infinitely many twin-prime pairs, or equivalently that \(T\) is infinite. Again, it suffices to prove that \(T\) is not bounded above. Suppose instead that some integer \(N\) is an upper bound for \(T\):
\[
r\le N\qquad\text{for every }r\in T.
\]
The number \(3\) belongs to \(T\), since \(3\) and \(5=3+2\) are prime. Therefore \(N\ge3\), so once more we may apply the factorial construction.

Choose \(x,y\ge1\) furnished by that construction, and now write
\[
p=6x-1,
\qquad r=6y-1,
\qquad q=6y+1=r+2.
\]
Here \(p\) and \(q\) are prime, \(r\in T\), and
\[
p+q=(N+2)!.
\]
Since \(r\in T\), the assumed upper bound gives
\[
r=6y-1\le N.
\]
It follows that
\[
q=r+2=6y+1\le N+2.
\]
The positive integer \(q\) therefore divides \((N+2)!\). Since it also divides itself, subtracting \(q\) from
\[
(N+2)!=p+q
\]
shows that
\[
q\mid p.
\]
The number \(p\) is prime, so a positive divisor of \(p\) must be either \(1\) or \(p\). Hence either \(q=1\) or \(q=p\).

Again both alternatives are impossible. Because \(y\ge1\),
\[
q=6y+1\ge7,
\]
so \(q\ne1\). If \(q=p\), then
\[
6y+1=6x-1,
\]
which yields
\[
6(x-y)=2,
\]
again impossible. Thus \(T\) cannot have an upper bound. Since every finite subset of \(\mathbb N\) is bounded above, \(T\) is infinite.

We have proved from the hypothesis \(a(n)>0\) for every \(n>1\) that the set of Sophie Germain primes and the set of twin-prime pairs are both infinite.
